title: The Pennsylvania Gazette, 2 October 1729
creator: Benjamin Franklin and Hugh Meredith (printers)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Sydney George Fisher, The True Benjamin Franklin, 5th edition (Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott, 1903; first published 1898)
caption: Front page of the first issue of the Pennsylvania Gazette printed by Benjamin Franklin and his partner Hugh Meredith (numbered 40, continuing the paper they had bought). Franklin's press later printed the official account of the 1744 Lancaster treaty, as it printed the Pennsylvania treaties of these years. The page is fifteen years older than the council and does not mention it.

title: Benjamin Franklin
creator: After David Martin
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Sydney George Fisher, The True Benjamin Franklin, 5th edition (Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott, 1903; first published 1898)
caption: Franklin reading at his desk beneath a bust of Isaac Newton, from the portrait David Martin painted in London in 1767. Franklin was 61, more than twenty years older than the printer who issued the Lancaster treaty in 1744; no portrait of him from the 1740s is reproduced here.

title: Mihšihkinaahkwa (Little Turtle)
creator: Unknown engraver, after a likeness traditionally said to derive from a lost portrait by Gilbert Stuart
date: Published 1909 (the likeness itself claimed to date from about 1797)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; public domain in the US.
original_holder: Charles H. L. Johnston, Famous Indian Chiefs (Boston: L. C. Page, 1909)
caption: Mihšihkinaahkwa (Little Turtle), the Myaamia (Miami) leader who spoke at length in the Greenville council of 1795 and signed the treaty. Johnston's 1909 book prints this engraving without naming its source. The same face has circulated since the nineteenth century as a copy of a Gilbert Stuart portrait painted about 1797 and since lost; that link, and how faithful the likeness is, cannot be confirmed.

title: Andrew Jackson
creator: Unknown engraver (source not named in the book); signature in facsimile below
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: William Garrott Brown, Andrew Jackson (Riverside Biographical Series; Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin, 1900)
caption: Andrew Jackson in old age, with his signature beneath, the frontispiece of a 1900 biography. Jackson was president when the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek was negotiated in September 1830, months after he signed the Indian Removal Act. The likeness shows him some fifteen years later; the book does not name the original.

title: Mosholatubbee and Peter Pitchlynn (Ha-tchoo-túc-knee)
creator: After George Catlin (hand-coloured engraving)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: George Catlin, Illustrations of the Manners, Customs, & Condition of the North American Indians, vol. II (London: Chatto & Windus, 1876; first published 1841 as Letters and Notes)
caption: Two Choctaw men painted by George Catlin in 1834 in the Choctaw country west of the Mississippi, after removal (his plates 221 and 222): the chief Mosholatubbee (Mó-sho-la-túb-bee, 'He who puts out and kills'), a signer of the 1830 treaty, who Catlin noted had since died of smallpox; and Peter Pitchlynn (Ha-tchoo-túc-knee, 'the Snapping Turtle'), whom Catlin calls 'Peter Pinchlin'. Catlin does not say which is which; by plate order Mosholatubbee is probably on the left. These are reduced engravings after his paintings.

title: Choctaw ball-play: ball up
creator: After George Catlin (hand-coloured engraving)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: George Catlin, Illustrations of the Manners, Customs, & Condition of the North American Indians, vol. II (London: Chatto & Windus, 1876; first published 1841 as Letters and Notes)
caption: Hundreds of players struggle for the ball between two sets of goal posts while spectators watch from the edge of the field: Catlin's view of a Choctaw ball game he attended near the Choctaw agency in the West in 1834, three years after the first removal parties left Mississippi. It is a reduced engraving after his painting.

title: U. States' Indian Frontier in 1840
creator: After George Catlin (map, hand-coloured)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: George Catlin, Illustrations of the Manners, Customs, & Condition of the North American Indians, vol. II (London: Chatto & Windus, 1876; first published 1841 as Letters and Notes)
caption: Catlin's map of the western frontier in 1840, 'showing the positions of the tribes that have been removed west of the Mississippi'. Coloured bands west of Arkansas and Missouri mark the lands assigned to removed nations, the Choctaw among them in the south, next to the Texas border.

title: John Pascoe Fawkner
creator: Unknown engraver
date: Published 1894 (Fawkner in old age; he died in 1869)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

caption: John Pascoe Fawkner, the Launceston publican and newspaperman whose party, sailing in the Enterprize, settled on the Yarra in August–September 1835 alongside Batman's men and disputed the 'treaty' claim. The engraving shows him as an old man, decades after 1835; the book does not give its source.

title: Collins Street, Melbourne, in 1840
creator: Unknown artist (engraving)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Alexander Sutherland and George Sutherland, The History of Australia and New Zealand from 1606 to 1890 (London and New York: Longmans, Green; Melbourne: George Robertson, 1894)
caption: Melbourne five years after Batman's deed: a broad unmade street lined with timber buildings, with a group of Aboriginal people seated in the foreground. The book dates the scene 1840 but does not name the artist or the original.

title: Mr. Busby's Residence, where the Treaty was signed
creator: Unknown photographer
date: Photograph of about 1914 or earlier; published 1914
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: T. Lindsay Buick, The Treaty of Waitangi, or How New Zealand Became a British Colony (Wellington: S. & W. Mackay, 1914)
caption: James Busby's house at Waitangi, on whose lawn te Tiriti was debated and first signed on 5–6 February 1840, as photographed for Buick's 1914 history. The house had been altered since 1840; the photograph is from the early twentieth century, not the time of the treaty.

title: Captain Hobson, R.N.
creator: Drawing for the book (signed J. McDonald), after an earlier portrait
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: T. Lindsay Buick, The Treaty of Waitangi, or How New Zealand Became a British Colony (Wellington: S. & W. Mackay, 1914)
caption: William Hobson, the naval captain sent as consul and lieutenant-governor, who put the treaty to the chiefs at Waitangi on 5 February 1840 and signed for the Crown. A pencil-style drawing made for Buick's book from an earlier portrait of Hobson in uniform; it is not a likeness drawn from life in 1840.

title: Tāmati Wāka Nene
creator: After a painting by Gottfried Lindauer
date: Painting late nineteenth century (after Nene's death in 1871); reproduced 1914
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: T. Lindsay Buick, The Treaty of Waitangi, or How New Zealand Became a British Colony (Wellington: S. & W. Mackay, 1914)
caption: Tāmati Wāka Nene of Ngāpuhi, whose speech in favour of the treaty at Waitangi on 5 February 1840 is remembered as turning the gathering, shown with a taiaha. Buick reproduced Lindauer's painting from the Partridge Collection; Lindauer worked decades after 1840, from photographs, so this is a posthumous portrait.

title: A Section of the Treaty Signatures
creator: Facsimile from one of the 1840 treaty sheets
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: T. Lindsay Buick, The Treaty of Waitangi, or How New Zealand Became a British Colony (Wellington: S. & W. Mackay, 1914)
caption: Names, moko and marks from one of the treaty sheets, reproduced by Buick: each name is preceded by 'Te Tohu o' ('the mark of'), and Te Rauparaha's mark and name appear near the top. Buick does not identify the sheet; Te Rauparaha signed twice in 1840, on the sheet carried south by Henry Williams (at Kapiti, in May) and on the Herald–Bunbury sheet (in June), so it is probably from one of those.

title: Winter 1851–52 in two Dakota winter counts
creator: Lakota (Dakota) winter-count keepers, as copied for Mallery (the "Corbusier winter counts")
why_public_domain: Published by the US Government Printing Office in an annual report of the Bureau of (American) Ethnology before 1929; a US government publication and public domain in the US.
original_holder: Garrick Mallery, Pictographs of the North American Indians: A Preliminary Paper, in Fourth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1882–83 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1886)
caption: The column for the winter of 1851–52, cut from Mallery's Plate XLVI and enlarged. In both counts the year is marked with a trade blanket standing for goods. Count I: 'They received their first annuities at the mouth of Horse Creek', the blanket ringed with marks for the people. Count II: 'Many goods were issued to them at Fort Laramie'. One keeper called it the 'Large-issue-of-goods-on-the-Platte-River winter'. These are copies made for the Bureau, not the originals.

title: Fort Laramie in 1849
creator: After a drawing made for Howard Stansbury's survey
why_public_domain: First published in 1852 in the report of a US Army survey; reproduced in a 1954 US government (National Park Service) handbook. Public domain in the US.
original_holder: David L. Hieb, Fort Laramie National Monument, Wyoming (National Park Service Historical Handbook Series No. 20; Washington: US Government Printing Office, 1954, reprint 1961); originally from Howard Stansbury, An Expedition to the Valley of the Great Salt Lake of Utah (1852)
caption: The old adobe Fort John on its bluff above the Laramie River, the year the Army bought it and made it Fort Laramie. The great council of 1851 was held not here but some 35 miles down the North Platte at the mouth of Horse Creek, because the grass near the fort could not feed the herds of the gathered nations.

title: Fort Laramie, Indian Territory, 1851
creator: National Park Service draughtsman, from a map by Lieut. A. J. Dowlson, Corps of Engineers
why_public_domain: A US government work: an 1851 Army engineer's map, redrawn by the National Park Service in 1954. Not subject to US copyright.
original_holder: David L. Hieb, Fort Laramie National Monument, Wyoming (National Park Service Historical Handbook Series No. 20; Washington: US Government Printing Office, 1954, reprint 1961)
caption: Plan of the post in the year of the treaty: the old adobe Fort John, officers' quarters ('Old Bedlam'), soldiers' quarters, stores, sutler's store and saw mill on the bend of the Laramie River. It is a 1954 redrawing of the 1851 map, not the original sheet.

title: Fort Laramie in 1853
creator: After a sketch by Frederick Piercy
why_public_domain: First published in 1855 (Piercy, Route from Liverpool to Great Salt Lake Valley); reproduced in a 1954 US government (National Park Service) handbook. Public domain in the US.
original_holder: David L. Hieb, Fort Laramie National Monument, Wyoming (National Park Service Historical Handbook Series No. 20; Washington: US Government Printing Office, 1954, reprint 1961); originally from Frederick Piercy, Route from Liverpool to Great Salt Lake Valley (Liverpool and London, 1855)
caption: The fort two summers after the treaty, seen across the flat by the English artist Frederick Piercy on his way to Utah: low buildings, the flagstaff and the bluffs behind. In 1854 the killing of Conquering Bear near here, in the Grattan fight, broke the peace the treaty had promised.

title: Set-t'aiñte (Satanta), White Bear
creator: William S. Soule (photographer)
why_public_domain: Published by the US Government Printing Office in an annual report of the Bureau of (American) Ethnology before 1929; a US government publication and public domain in the US.
original_holder: James Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians, in Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1895–96, part 1 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1898)
caption: Set-t'aiñte (Satanta), the Kiowa leader whose speeches at Medicine Lodge Creek in October 1867 were widely reported, photographed about three years later wearing a peace medal on a ribbon and an army coat. Mooney's Figure 45.

title: Sét-t'án (Little Bear)
creator: Drawing made for the report (artist's initials on the plate)
why_public_domain: Published by the US Government Printing Office in an annual report of the Bureau of (American) Ethnology before 1929; a US government publication and public domain in the US.
original_holder: James Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians, in Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1895–96, part 1 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1898)
caption: Sét-t'án (Little Bear), the Kiowa keeper of the annual calendar Mooney published, which marks the winter of 1867–68 with the Medicine Lodge treaty. A drawn portrait from Mooney's Figure 61, probably made from a photograph in the 1890s.

title: Winter 1867–68 in the Set-t'an calendar: the Medicine Lodge treaty
creator: Sét-t'án (Kiowa calendar keeper); copied for Mooney's report
why_public_domain: Published by the US Government Printing Office in an annual report of the Bureau of (American) Ethnology before 1929; a US government publication and public domain in the US.
original_holder: James Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians, in Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1895–96, part 1 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1898)
caption: Mooney's Figure 142. The Kiowa called this 'Timber-hill winter' after the treaty made on Medicine Lodge Creek (Ä´yä´daldä P'a, 'Timber-hill river'). The black bar is the winter mark; above it a man in a hat, apparently a soldier, shakes hands with a Kiowa, under a tree-covered hill naming the place. A copy of the calendar drawing, not the original.

title: Gui-pägo (Lone Wolf the younger)
creator: Photograph by Bell
why_public_domain: Published by the US Government Printing Office in an annual report of the Bureau of (American) Ethnology before 1929; a US government publication and public domain in the US.
original_holder: James Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians, in Seventeenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1895–96, part 1 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1898)
caption: Gui-pägo, Lone Wolf, whom Mooney in 1898 called 'present head-chief of the Kiowa': successor to the name of the Lone Wolf who signed at Medicine Lodge in 1867, and usually described as his adopted son. As principal plaintiff he took the allotment of Kiowa land to the US Supreme Court, which ruled against him in Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903). Photographed in 1888.

title: The Great Lone Land: route of Captain W. F. Butler
creator: Map published with the book
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: William Francis Butler, The Great Lone Land: A Narrative of Travel and Adventure in the North-West of America (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Low & Searle, 1872)
caption: Map of British North America from Lake Superior to the Rocky Mountains, with the route Butler travelled in 1870–71 when sent to report on the Saskatchewan country, past Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt, where Treaty 6 was negotiated five years later. His report urged that a mounted force be sent to the Saskatchewan.

title: The Forks of the Saskatchewan
creator: Engraving after a sketch from Butler's journey (artist not named)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: William Francis Butler, The Great Lone Land: A Narrative of Travel and Adventure in the North-West of America (London: Sampson Low, Marston, Low & Searle, 1872)
caption: The meeting of the North and South Saskatchewan rivers in winter, below Fort Carlton, as engraved for Butler's account of his 1870–71 journey. The Treaty 6 country lay upstream along both branches.

title: Indians receiving treaty payment on prairie
creator: Unknown photographer
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; public domain in the US.
original_holder: R. G. MacBeth, Policing the Plains: Being the Real-Life Record of the Famous Royal North-West Mounted Police (London, New York and Toronto: Hodder and Stoughton, 1921)
caption: People seated before a tent flying the Union flag at an annual treaty payment, when each person received the cash annuity promised under the numbered treaties (five dollars a head under Treaty 6). The book gives no date, place or treaty, so this may not be a Treaty 6 payment.

title: Official residence of Bismarck in Berlin
creator: Unknown engraver
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

caption: The chancellor's palace at Wilhelmstraße 77, where the Berlin (Congo) Conference opened on 15 November 1884 and sat until the General Act was signed on 26 February 1885. No African ruler or envoy was present. An engraving from a biography of Bismarck; its date is not given.

title: Bismarck
creator: After a painting by Franz von Lenbach
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: James Wycliffe Headlam, Bismarck and the Foundation of the German Empire (Heroes of the Nations; New York and London: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1899)
caption: Otto von Bismarck in a cuirassier's helmet and uniform, one of the many portraits Lenbach painted of him. Bismarck hosted and chaired the Berlin Conference. The book does not date the painting.

title: Manga Bell's palace, Duala
creator: Unknown photographer
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Albert F. Calvert, The Cameroons (London: T. Werner Laurie, 1917)
caption: The two-storey house with verandas and a pagoda-like tower that Calvert labels 'Manga Beli's Palace', the residence of the Bell family, whose head King Ndumbe Lobe Bell signed the July 1884 treaty placing Duala under German protection. The building, now known as La Pagode, was put up in the German period about twenty years later, so it shows the colony the treaty made, not the Duala of 1884.

title: Outline Map of Africa
creator: Map published with the book
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

caption: Africa twenty years after the Berlin Conference, marked with the claims of the European powers and, at the centre, the boundary of the Congo Free State that the conference's powers recognised as King Leopold's. The map is from a 1905 book written in defence of Leopold's state.

title: Part of Matabele, Mashona and Manica Land
creator: Map from the Proceedings of the Royal Geographical Society, reproduced in the book
date: Journeys of 1891; first published 1892; this edition 1895
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: J. Theodore Bent, The Ruined Cities of Mashonaland: Being a Record of Excavation and Exploration in 1891, new edition (London: Longmans, Green, 1895; first edition 1892)
caption: Map of the country east of Lobengula's kingdom, with routes in red, made three years after the Rudd Concession, when the British South Africa Company's pioneer column (1890) had already occupied Mashonaland under the concession. Matabeleland lies at the western edge. It shows the surveyors' view of the land, not the Ndebele one.
